## The scene unit

### The Value Turn

**Also called:** the charge change, scene polarity shift, the reversal
**What it is:** A value in the scene — trust, safety, hope, control, love, freedom — stands at one charge when the scene opens and the opposite charge when it closes. Nothing else defines a scene. If the value is the same at the end as at the start, what you have is an event, not a scene.
**Effect on the audience:** Forward motion without visible mechanics. The audience cannot name what moved, but they feel the floor tilt, and they will follow a story that tilts and abandon one that stays level.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every dramatic form. The most useful place to apply it is the scene you suspect is dead: name the value, mark its charge on the first page and the last, and if they match you have found why the scene feels flat. It is the fastest diagnostic in the craft and the only one that works on someone else's draft as well as your own.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** Non-dramatic forms that run on accumulation rather than change — a lyric poem, a concept music video, an observational passage, a tone piece, a Kishōtenketsu development section. Forcing a turn on them flattens what they were built to do. Also beware turning the same value in every scene: fifteen scenes that each move trust from up to down is one scene written fifteen times.
**Example:**
> Open: she has the keys in her hand and he is asking her to stay. *Control: hers.*
> Close: she is still holding the keys, and he has stopped asking. *Control: his.*
> Not one line of dialogue announced the shift.

**Yields to:** `scene.kishotenketsu_scene` — Form runs on accumulation, not on charge change.  
`scene.value_turn`

### Scene and Sequel

**Also called:** the Swain pair, action unit and reaction unit
**What it is:** Two alternating unit types. A **scene** runs Goal → Conflict → Disaster: the character wants something, is opposed, and ends worse off. A **sequel** runs Reaction → Dilemma → Decision: the character absorbs the disaster, finds every option bad, and chooses one — which becomes the goal of the next scene.
**Effect on the audience:** Causality they can feel. The chain is unbreakable, because each sequel's decision is the next scene's goal, which makes it structurally impossible to write events that merely follow one another.
**Used for and where it works best:** Prose above all, where it was developed, and any draft that feels episodic. If a reader says "things happen but I'm not gripped", the sequels are almost certainly missing — the character is being moved through plot without ever choosing. It is also the correct fix for a protagonist who reads as passive: they are not passive, they have simply never been shown deciding.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Feature Film, Limited Series, Game Narrative, Comics | genres: Thriller, Crime, Adventure, Drama, Romance, Fantasy, Science Fiction
**Avoid when:** Fast-paced screen formats where full sequels kill momentum — in action and in short-form the sequel compresses to a single look, a held beat, one line. The unit still exists; it just gets three seconds instead of three pages. Also avoid in ensemble work, where cutting away is itself the sequel.
**Example:**
> **Scene:** She goes to the bank to stop the transfer. *Goal.* It was authorised this morning. *Conflict.* By her brother. *Disaster.*
> **Sequel:** She sits in the car park. *Reaction.* Call him, or call the police, or say nothing and lose the flat. *Dilemma.* She drives to his house. *Decision — and the next scene's goal.*

**Yields to:** `scene.crosscut_pair` — Ensemble work: cutting away is the sequel.  
`scene.scene_and_sequel`

### Goal, Conflict, Disaster

**Also called:** GCD, the action unit
**What it is:** The scene's three-part spine. The viewpoint character enters with a specific, achievable want; something concrete opposes it; and the scene ends not in failure but in something worse or more complicated than failure.
**Effect on the audience:** Tension with a shape. The audience knows what is being attempted, so they can want it — and a disaster is only felt by an audience that wanted the goal.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any scene that is currently a conversation. The most common repair in the craft: give the viewpoint character one concrete thing they are trying to get from the other person in the next five minutes, and the scene organises itself. The goal must be scene-sized, not story-sized: not "win his respect" but "get him to sign this today".
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: Thriller, Crime, Drama, Adventure, Romance, Procedural, Action
**Avoid when:** The disaster is arbitrary. A disaster that could not have been produced by the goal is a coincidence, and coincidence against the protagonist reads as authorial cruelty. The best disaster is caused by the attempt itself.
**Example:**
> **Goal:** persuade the old man to sell.
> **Conflict:** he has already refused three buyers and enjoys refusing.
> **Disaster:** he agrees — on condition she stays and runs it.

**Yields to:** `scene.kishotenketsu_scene` — Nobody in the scene can want anything.  
`scene.goal_conflict_disaster`

### Reaction, Dilemma, Decision

**Also called:** RDD, the sequel unit
**What it is:** The scene after the scene. The character reacts emotionally and physically, then confronts a dilemma in which every available option is bad, then chooses.
**Effect on the audience:** Attachment. The audience bonds to a character in the sequel, not in the scene — watching someone act is interesting, watching them weigh is intimate.
**Used for and where it works best:** After every major disaster, and especially before any decision the audience might otherwise find implausible. A choice the audience has watched a character agonise over is accepted; the same choice made off-page is questioned. The dilemma must contain no good option: if one branch is obviously right, there is no dilemma and the character is merely slow.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Short Story, Game Narrative, Memoir | genres: Drama, Tragedy, Romance, Crime, Psychological, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** Momentum matters more than interiority — chases, comedies of pace, short-form. Compress rather than cut: the reaction becomes a breath, the dilemma becomes an object in the hand, the decision becomes a direction taken.
**Example:**
> She sits with the phone face down. *Reaction.*
> Tell their mother and destroy him; say nothing and become part of it; or leave the city tonight. *Dilemma.*
> She turns the phone over. *Decision.*

`scene.reaction_dilemma_decision`

### The Motivation-Reaction Unit

**Also called:** MRU, stimulus and response, the Swain sentence pair
**What it is:** At the sentence level, a chain of external motivation followed by the viewpoint character's reaction, in strict order: feeling first, then reflex, then action, then speech. When the motivations or reactions run out, the scene is over.
**Effect on the audience:** Immersion at the smallest available scale. Reading in this order matches the order experience actually arrives in, so the prose disappears.
**Used for and where it works best:** Deep third-person and first-person prose, action sequences, and any passage that feels reported rather than experienced. It is the smallest unit in the entire database — the camera has nothing below the shot, but writing goes down to the order of two clauses. The single most common prose error it fixes: writing the action before the feeling, which tells the reader what happened instead of letting them have it.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Interactive Fiction, Audio Drama | genres: Thriller, Horror, Romance, Literary, Crime, Adventure
**Avoid when:** Distant or ironic narration, essay, and most screenwriting — a screenplay has no access to interiority and the order belongs to the edit. Also avoid running it for pages: strict MRU chains become mechanical, and experienced prose breaks the pattern deliberately at moments of shock.
**Example:**
> **Wrong order:** She ran for the door, terrified, as the lock turned.
> **MRU order:** The lock turned. Cold went through her hands. She was moving before she decided to. "Not this time."

`scene.mru`

### Reversal of Power

**Also called:** the status flip, the power turn
**What it is:** One of the two McKee reversal types. The relative power of the viewpoint character and another character in the scene swaps between the opening and the close.
**Effect on the audience:** Precise satisfaction. Power is the value an audience tracks most accurately without being told, so a power reversal reads clean even when the subject matter is complex.
**Used for and where it works best:** Interrogations, negotiations, family confrontations, job scenes, any two-hander. Pair it with `dial.question_control` — move the questions across the scene and the power moves with them. The reversal must be produced by something the weaker party does, not by information arriving from outside; luck changes circumstances, not power.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: Crime, Courtroom, Political, Drama, Workplace, Thriller, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The scene is about two people failing to connect rather than competing. Not every scene is a contest, and imposing a power reversal on an intimacy scene turns tenderness into strategy.
**Example:**
> He begins behind the desk and she stands. He ends standing, and she has not sat down either — but she is the one holding the folder now.

**Yields to:** `scene.reversal_of_expectation` — The scene is not a contest.  
`scene.reversal_of_power`

### Reversal of Expectation

**Also called:** the expectation turn, the wrong outcome
**What it is:** The second McKee reversal type. The viewpoint character enters the scene expecting one outcome and encounters a different one — not necessarily worse, and often better in a way that costs more.
**Effect on the audience:** Alertness. Once a story has taught an audience that expectations do not resolve, they stop predicting and start watching.
**Used for and where it works best:** Midpoints, and anywhere the story has become predictable. The strongest version is a granted wish: the character gets exactly what they asked for, and the scene's disaster is that they now have it. Use it sparingly enough that the audience still forms expectations — a story with no reliable outcomes stops producing them, and the technique dies of its own success.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: Drama, Thriller, Comedy, Crime, Romance, Satire, Tragedy
**Avoid when:** The audience's expectation has not been established. A reversal requires a clearly planted expectation to reverse, and writers routinely skip the planting because they already know what is coming.
**Example:**
> She goes to the hospital prepared to fight for the room.
> They give her the room immediately, because there is no longer any reason not to.

**Yields to:** `scene.reversal_of_power` — No expectation was planted to reverse.  
`scene.reversal_of_expectation`

### The Scene Question

**Also called:** the dramatic question at scene level, the open hook
**What it is:** Each scene raises one specific question in the audience's mind — will he sign, does she know, is the money there — and either answers it and raises a new one, or hands it forward unanswered.
**Effect on the audience:** Continuous pull. Attention is sustained by open questions, not by interest in the characters, which is why a sympathetic cast in a question-less story still loses the room.
**Used for and where it works best:** Structural diagnosis across a whole draft. Write the question each scene raises in a single column; wherever two consecutive scenes raise the same question, one of them is redundant, and wherever a scene raises none, it is inert. This is the most efficient full-draft audit available and takes about an hour on a feature.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** Never avoid as a diagnostic. But do not answer every question in the scene that raises it — a work in which each scene closes its own question reads as a sequence of episodes rather than a story.
**Example:**
> Scene 12 asks: will the brother admit he was there?
> Scene 13 does not answer it. It asks who else was.
> Scene 19 answers the first one, and by then it means something different.

`scene.scene_question`

## Entry and exit

### Late Entry

**Also called:** enter late, in medias res at scene level
**What it is:** The scene begins after it has started. The arrival, the greeting and the establishment of why these people are in a room together are all removed, and the first line is one that could not have been predicted from the setup.
**Effect on the audience:** Momentum and respect. Being dropped mid-situation flatters an audience; being walked in flatters no one.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every dramatic format, and the first thing to try on a scene that feels slow. The reliable test: cut the first three lines of every scene in a draft and read it again — in most cases nothing is lost and the whole thing quickens. In short-form it stops being a choice and becomes a condition, because vertical micro-drama and reels have no runtime for arrival at all.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The arrival is the scene — someone entering a place they are not welcome, a homecoming, a first meeting whose awkwardness is the content. Also be careful in prose across many locations, where cutting every arrival can leave a reader spatially lost; keep one anchoring line.
**Example:**
> **Before:** He parks. He walks up. He knocks. She opens. "Come in." "Thanks." They sit. "So what did the lawyer say?"
> **After:** "So what did the lawyer say?"

**Yields to:** `scene.arrival_scene` — where the arrival *is* the scene: a homecoming, someone entering a place they are not welcome, a first meeting whose awkwardness is the content.  
`scene.late_entry`

### Early Exit

**Also called:** leave early, cutting before the conclusion
**What it is:** The scene ends before its conversation finishes — on the turn, not after it. The audience does not see the characters absorb what happened, agree on what it means, or say goodbye.
**Effect on the audience:** The scene keeps working after it stops. An audience denied the wind-down completes it themselves, which transfers the scene from the screen into their head.
**Used for and where it works best:** Everywhere, and particularly on any scene whose last quarter is characters agreeing about what just happened. The instruction is mechanical and almost always right: find the moment the value turns, keep one beat after it, delete the rest. In serial short-form this is the button, cut two seconds earlier than feels safe.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The scene's meaning lives in the aftermath rather than the event — a death scene, a confession, anything where the reaction is the content. There, hold past comfort instead; the rule is not "always cut early" but "never cut late".
**Example:**
> "You knew."
> "I knew."
>
> **[cut]** — not "Why didn't you tell me?" and everything that follows.

**Yields to:** `scene.held_exit` — where the meaning lives in the aftermath rather than the event: a death scene, a confession, anything where the reaction is the content. The rule is never *cut early*, it is *never cut late*.  
`scene.early_exit`

### Entering on the Answer

**Also called:** the pre-lapped entry, arriving mid-reply
**What it is:** A more aggressive late entry: the scene opens on the answer to a question the audience never heard, and they reconstruct the question from the reply.
**Effect on the audience:** Instant engagement plus a small puzzle. The audience is working within the first two seconds, which is precisely where short-form audiences are decided.
**Used for and where it works best:** Openings of episodes and of short-form pieces, and any point in a feature where the pace has become even. It is the single strongest scene-opening device for reels and vertical drama because it costs nothing and buys the first second. The reconstructed question must be inferable within about one line, or the audience is lost rather than intrigued.
**Best in:** formats: Vertical Micro-Drama, Reels/Shorts, One-Hour Drama, Feature Film, Podcast, Half-Hour Comedy | genres: Thriller, Crime, Comedy, Melodrama, Political, Drama
**Avoid when:** Used more than once or twice in a work, where it becomes a tic — a whole film of scenes opening mid-reply reads as a style rather than a choice. Also avoid when the withheld question carries plot-critical information.
**Example:**
> **Opening line of the episode:**
> "Because she asked me not to, that's why."

**Yields to:** `scene.opening_on_reaction` — Repeated use, or the question carries plot.  
`scene.entering_on_the_answer`

### The Held Exit

**Also called:** staying past comfort, the extended close
**What it is:** The inverse of the early exit, used deliberately. The scene stays after the event, on a character doing something ordinary, for longer than the audience expects.
**Effect on the audience:** Weight. Duration is the only tool that can make an audience feel the size of something, and a held ending converts an event into a consequence.
**Used for and where it works best:** After a death, a departure, a verdict, a diagnosis. The hold must be on a physical action, not on a face doing nothing — someone washing a cup, folding a coat, waiting for a kettle. It is also the technique that most distinguishes a written scene from a generated one: an ordinary action after a large event is a choice no formula produces. In heritage and documentary work it is often the only place real grief can sit.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Short Film, Documentary, Stage Play | genres: Drama, Tragedy, War, Family Drama, Heritage, Literary
**Avoid when:** Anywhere the format cannot afford seconds — advertising, reels, micro-drama — and anywhere it has already been used recently. A held ending is a resource that depletes: the second one in twenty minutes is half as strong, and the third is pacing failure.
**Example:**
> After the ambulance leaves, she goes back inside and puts the chairs back around the table. All six of them. Then she sits down.

**Yields to:** `scene.early_exit` — The format cannot afford the held seconds.  
`scene.held_exit`

### The Interrupted Scene

**Also called:** the broken scene, denying the conclusion
**What it is:** A scene is cut off by an external event — an arrival, a phone, an alarm — before its business is done, and the business is never resumed on the page.
**Effect on the audience:** Frustration transferred into forward pressure. The audience carries the unfinished scene as an open loop.
**Used for and where it works best:** When a scene would resolve something you need unresolved, and you cannot justify the characters simply stopping. It is also the honest way to write lives that do not permit completion — parents, medical staff, people in crisis — where being interrupted is not a device but the condition. Use the interruption to characterise: what interrupts a person tells the audience what owns them.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Feature Film, Novel, Vertical Micro-Drama, Half-Hour Comedy | genres: Family Drama, Medical, Crime, Social Drama, Comedy, Thriller
**Avoid when:** It is used to escape a scene the writer has not solved. Audiences can feel the difference between a character being interrupted and a writer being rescued, and the tell is that nothing was at stake in the part that did play.
**Example:**
> "There's something I need to tell you before Mama gets here—"
>
> *The front door.*

**Yields to:** `scene.third_attack` — You are escaping a scene you never solved.  
`scene.interrupted_scene`

## Escalation

### Tactic Change

**Also called:** the new approach, shifting the attack
**What it is:** Within one scene, a character who wants something tries one method, fails, and switches to a different one — charm, then reason, then guilt, then threat. The want stays constant; only the means change.
**Effect on the audience:** The sensation of a scene going somewhere, which is almost entirely produced by this one mechanism. Most scenes that feel repetitive are scenes where a character repeats a tactic rather than changing it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any scene longer than a page. This is the primary engine of scene-level escalation, and it is more useful than raising volume or stakes, because a tactic change reveals character: the order in which someone reaches for their tools is who they are. Plan three tactics before writing and let the third be the one that costs them something to use.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The character has only one tool and that is the point — some characters are dramatic precisely because they cannot change tactic. There, let the failure repeat, and make the other character's growing discomfort carry the escalation instead.
**Example:**
> "You'd be doing me a favour." *Charm.*
> "It's four days' work, that's all it is." *Reason.*
> "After what your father did for mine." *Guilt.*
> "I still have the letters." *Threat.*

**Yields to:** `scene.barrier_mid_scene` — Character has one tool; escalate from the room.  
`scene.tactic_change`

### Escalating Cost

**Also called:** the rising price, each attempt costs more
**What it is:** Across a sequence of scenes, each successive attempt to reach the goal requires the character to spend something larger — money, then reputation, then a relationship, then a principle.
**Effect on the audience:** Mounting dread, and a clean read on character. What a person is willing to spend next is the most legible measure of how much they want something.
**Used for and where it works best:** Second acts, which are the place drafts most often stall. The failure mode it fixes: obstacles that are merely bigger rather than more expensive. A larger obstacle raises difficulty; a larger cost raises meaning. Design the ladder before drafting, ending with the thing the character said in Act One they would never do.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Limited Series, One-Hour Drama, Game Narrative | genres: Crime, Drama, Thriller, Tragedy, Gangster, Sports, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** Comedies of repetition, where the joke is that nothing escalates, and procedurals designed to reset each week. Also avoid escalating past the character's plausible limit — a cost the audience does not believe they would pay breaks the person rather than the scene.
**Example:**
> He borrows from the shop. Then from his sister. Then he signs for the flat. Then he tells the police it was Nabil.

`scene.escalating_cost`

### The Barrier Introduced Mid-Scene

**Also called:** the late obstacle, the complication that arrives
**What it is:** A physical or social obstacle appears partway through a scene that was already running — a locked door, a returning spouse, a witness, a power cut — and the characters must finish their business around it.
**Effect on the audience:** Renewed attention at exactly the point where a scene normally sags: the middle.
**Used for and where it works best:** Long scenes, particularly two-handers that must run for several pages. The barrier should constrain *how* they can speak rather than *whether* they can — a witness arriving forces the argument into code, which is more interesting than ending it. This also generates subtext mechanically, which makes it one of the few techniques that produces craft rather than requiring it.
**Best in:** formats: Stage Play, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Half-Hour Comedy | genres: Drama, Comedy, Crime, Farce, Thriller, Family Drama, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The scene is already short, or the barrier has no relationship to the scene's content. An arbitrary complication is a distraction; the best barrier is one the characters' own behaviour caused.
**Example:**
> They are halfway through the argument when the daughter comes down for water. They continue it in full voice, about the car.

**Yields to:** `scene.third_party_arrival` — Use a person with a stake, not an obstacle.  
`scene.barrier_mid_scene`

### The Third Party Arrival

**Also called:** the entering character, the triangle
**What it is:** A third person enters a two-hander, converting a private exchange into a performance and altering what each character can say.
**Effect on the audience:** Immediate complexity. Two people negotiate; three people take sides, and the audience begins tracking alliances.
**Used for and where it works best:** Scenes that have reached deadlock, and any moment where you need subtext without writing it — the arrival creates it for free, because both original characters must now encode. The arriving character does not need dialogue; presence alone does the work. It also enables `dial.talking_to_the_room`, which requires a third body.
**Best in:** formats: Stage Play, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Half-Hour Comedy | genres: Family Drama, Social Drama, Comedy, Crime, Political, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The third party has no stake. A character who wanders in, is present, and wanders out drains a scene rather than complicating it — the entrant must change what is possible.
**Example:**
> They have been arguing about the money for three minutes when the mother comes in with the tray, and for the next two minutes they discuss the weather with complete conviction.

**Yields to:** `scene.before_a_stranger` — The third person has no stake.  
`scene.third_party_arrival`

### The Granted Wish

**Also called:** yes-and-disaster, winning wrong
**What it is:** The character achieves the scene goal completely, and the achievement is the disaster.
**Effect on the audience:** Unease that outlasts the scene. A denied goal produces sympathy; a granted one produces dread, because the audience now has to watch the consequences arrive.
**Used for and where it works best:** Midpoints, and any story about desire rather than obstacle — ambition, addiction, revenge, romance. It is also the most effective single answer to a second act built on repeated refusals, which is the most common structural monotony in drafts. Grant the thing early and the story gets harder rather than easier.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Limited Series, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play | genres: Tragedy, Crime, Drama, Psychological, Gangster, Romance, Satire
**Avoid when:** The audience does not yet want the goal. Granting a wish the audience has not invested in produces nothing; the technique is entirely powered by the wanting that preceded it.
**Example:**
> They give her the promotion. The office is her father's. The staff are the ones who testified against him.

**Yields to:** `scene.goal_conflict_disaster` — Audience has not yet invested in the want.  
`scene.granted_wish`

## Diagnosis and repair

### The Dead Scene Test

**Also called:** the three-column audit, scene triage
**What it is:** A diagnostic rather than a technique. For any suspect scene, answer three questions: what does the viewpoint character want *in this scene*; what value turns, and in which direction; and what is different at the end. A scene that cannot answer all three is not a scene.
**Effect on the work:** It locates the fault instead of describing the symptom. "This scene is boring" is not actionable; "nobody wants anything" is.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every draft after the first, and on notes received from other people — most notes describe symptoms, and this converts them into causes. A scene that fails the test has exactly four futures, in this order of preference: give it a want, merge it with the scene beside it, move its information into a scene that works, or delete it.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The first draft. Running diagnostics while generating is the most reliable way to stop generating.
**Example:**
> **Want:** none — they are catching up.
> **Turn:** none.
> **Different at the end:** the audience knows about the brother.
> **Verdict:** not a scene. Move the brother into scene 14, where somebody wants something.

`scene.dead_scene_test`

### Give Someone Something to Want

**Also called:** the want injection, the immediate agenda
**What it is:** The primary repair for a dead scene. Assign the viewpoint character one concrete, scene-sized thing to obtain from the other person before the scene ends, and let the other person have a reason to withhold it.
**Effect on the work:** The scene reorganises itself around the want, usually without rewriting the dialogue — the same lines read differently once one party is trying to get something.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any conversation scene, exposition scene or "catching up" scene. The want must be achievable in the room and specific enough to fail: not understanding, not closure, but the address, the signature, the admission, the key, the money by Thursday. If you cannot name the object, you do not yet have a want.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The scene is deliberately a sequel — reaction, dilemma, decision — which runs on weighing rather than wanting. Adding a want there destroys the pause the structure needed.
**Example:**
> **Before:** Two brothers talk about their childhood.
> **After:** Two brothers talk about their childhood, and one of them is waiting for the other to offer him the spare room without having to ask.

**Yields to:** `scene.reaction_dilemma_decision` — where the scene is deliberately a sequel, which runs on weighing rather than wanting; a want there destroys the pause the structure needed.  
`scene.give_a_want`

### Transplant the Scene

**Also called:** change the location, the wrong room
**What it is:** Move a scene out of the neutral room it was written in — living room, office, café — and into a location that constrains, exposes or embarrasses the characters. The dialogue often survives unchanged.
**Effect on the audience:** Texture and subtext for free. What the characters must do with their bodies while speaking becomes available as a second channel.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any draft in which several scenes take place sitting down indoors. The strongest transplants are places where one character has authority and the other does not — a barber's chair, a hospital corridor, a mosque courtyard, a car with one person driving. In low-budget and AI-generated production this is also the cheapest way to make a script look expensive: the same exchange in a queue is worth more than the same exchange on a sofa.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Short Film, Vertical Micro-Drama, Novel, Reels/Shorts | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The neutral room is the point — some scenes are about the domestic flatness of the setting, and a striking location would argue against the content.
**Example:**
> The break-up, moved from her flat to the passenger seat of his car in a car park, with the engine running and neither of them putting on a seatbelt.

**Yields to:** `scene.swap_who_wants` — The neutral room is the point.  
`scene.transplant`

### Swap Who Wants It

**Also called:** reversing the agenda, moving the need
**What it is:** Take a scene where character A is pursuing character B and reverse it: B now wants something from A, while A holds what B needs.
**Effect on the work:** A scene that was predictable becomes unfamiliar, usually while keeping its plot function intact. The information still gets delivered; only the pressure moves.
**Used for and where it works best:** Scenes that feel obligatory — the one where the detective interviews the widow, the one where the hero asks the mentor for help. Reversing who needs what converts a scene the audience has seen before into one they have not. Try it as an experiment on any scene you are dreading writing; the dread usually means you already know how it goes.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The power relationship is load-bearing for the story's argument. Reversing a scene about institutional power so that the institution needs something from the individual may be a better scene and a false one.
**Example:**
> **Written:** the son asks the father for the money.
> **Swapped:** the father needs the son to take the money, and the son will not.

**Yields to:** `scene.transplant` — The power relationship is load-bearing.  
`scene.swap_who_wants`

### Merge Two Scenes

**Also called:** collapsing scenes, the combined beat
**What it is:** Two adjacent scenes that each perform one function are combined into a single scene performing both, usually by putting the two conversations in the same room at the same time.
**Effect on the work:** Density. A scene doing two jobs is nearly always better than two scenes doing one each, because the two jobs interfere with each other and interference is drama.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any draft that is long, or any sequence that feels like a list. It is the most reliable way to cut length without cutting content, which is the note every writer eventually receives. Look specifically for two consecutive scenes with the same location or the same pair of characters — those merge almost automatically.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Short Film, Vertical Micro-Drama | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The two functions require different emotional registers and the merge would blunt both. Some information genuinely needs its own air, and a merged scene that does two things badly is worse than two that each do one well.
**Example:**
> **Before:** Scene 22, she learns the clinic has closed. Scene 23, she tells her mother she is leaving.
> **After:** She tells her mother she is leaving, and takes the call about the clinic in the middle of it.

**Yields to:** `scene.absorb_and_delete` — Registers clash; redistribute instead.  
`scene.merge_two_scenes`

### Absorb and Delete

**Also called:** redistributing the scene, the removed link
**What it is:** A scene that carries only information is deleted, and its information is redistributed into scenes that already have dramatic life — usually as a fragment inside an argument or a correction.
**Effect on the work:** Pace, and the disappearance of the "connective" scenes that make a draft feel administrative.
**Used for and where it works best:** After the dead scene test has failed a scene that nevertheless contains something the audience needs. Pair it with `dial.exposition_accusation` or `dial.exposition_correction`, which are the two vehicles the absorbed information should travel in. The test after deletion: read the neighbouring scenes in sequence and check that nothing is now unexplained; if nothing is, the scene was a habit.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The information is large enough that absorbing it distorts its host. Some facts need a scene; the mistake is assuming most do.
**Example:**
> Delete the scene where the doctor explains the prognosis. Move the prognosis into the argument two scenes later, where the sister uses it as a weapon.

**Yields to:** `scene.merge_two_scenes` — The information is too large to absorb.  
`scene.absorb_and_delete`

---

## Scene shapes

### The Trap Scene

**Also called:** the closed room, nobody can leave
**What it is:** A scene in which the characters are prevented from exiting by something plausible — a car in motion, a funeral, a queue, a surgery, a family dinner, a delayed flight — so the conversation must continue past the point where either would normally end it.
**Effect on the audience:** Escalating discomfort with no release valve. The audience knows nobody can walk out, so every line lands harder than it would in a room with a door.
**Used for and where it works best:** The scene where something must finally be said. It is the most reliable pressure-generating shape in the craft, and it is why so many decisive scenes in film happen in cars. The trap must be socially rather than physically enforced where possible — a locked door is a thriller, a wedding is a tragedy.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Stage Play, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Short Film, Vertical Micro-Drama | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Thriller, Crime, Tragedy, Comedy, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The trap is not believable for these specific people — a character who would simply leave, and whom the audience knows would simply leave, makes the writer visible.
**Example:**
> Forty minutes in a car to the airport. He has known since Tuesday. She asks him, at the second roundabout, why he has not asked about Tuesday.

**Yields to:** `scene.ticking_scene` — These people would simply leave.  
`scene.trap_scene`

### The Ticking Scene

**Also called:** the clock scene, the deadline in the room
**What it is:** A visible, specific limit runs inside the scene — a boiling pot, a boarding call, a meter, a prayer about to begin, a battery at four per cent — and the characters' business must conclude before it expires.
**Effect on the audience:** Involuntary attention. A visible clock recruits the audience's own anxiety, which is a resource no amount of dialogue can buy.
**Used for and where it works best:** Scenes carrying necessary but undramatic content — instructions, plans, explanations. A clock makes exposition urgent without making it aggressive, which is the alternative solution when accusation does not fit. The limit must be concrete and observable by the audience, not merely asserted.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Vertical Micro-Drama, Game Narrative, Reels/Shorts | genres: Thriller, Crime, Action, Medical, Heist, Comedy, Drama
**Avoid when:** The scene needs reflection. A clock forbids interiority; it is the enemy of the sequel, and putting one in a decision scene produces a character who chooses because time ran out, which is not a choice.
**Example:**
> She explains the whole arrangement while the rice cooks. When it is done, she serves it, and nothing more is said about it that night.

**Yields to:** `scene.reaction_dilemma_decision` — where the scene needs reflection. A clock forbids interiority and produces a character who chooses because time ran out, which is not a choice.  
`scene.ticking_scene`

### The Public Scene

**Also called:** the witnessed exchange, the audience within
**What it is:** A private conflict conducted in a place where other people can see or hear, forcing both parties to maintain a surface while fighting underneath it.
**Effect on the audience:** Double vision. They watch two conversations at once — the one the room can hear and the one only they can — and the gap between them is the pleasure.
**Used for and where it works best:** Cultures and families where public dignity is itself a value, which is most of them. It generates subtext structurally rather than requiring the writer to invent it. It is also the strongest shape for a scene in which one party has power and the other has only the leverage of embarrassment.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Stage Play, One-Hour Drama, Novel | genres: Family Drama, Social Drama, Heritage, Comedy, Tragedy, Political, Historical
**Avoid when:** The characters have no reason to preserve appearances. A public scene between two people who do not care who hears is just a loud scene.
**Example:**
> At the engagement party, in front of forty guests, she asks him — smiling, holding his arm — whether he has told his mother where the money came from.

**Yields to:** `scene.aimed_through_the_room` — Only one party may speak.  
`scene.public_scene`

### The Transaction Scene

**Also called:** the exchange, the negotiation shape
**What it is:** A scene organised around something physically changing hands — money, keys, documents, a child, a body, a dish. The object's movement is the scene's structure.
**Effect on the audience:** Clarity and weight. An audience tracks an object more reliably than an argument, and an object that has moved cannot move back.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any scene about a decision that must feel irreversible. It also solves the problem of writing a scene whose content is abstract — a betrayal, a forgiveness, an abandonment — by making the abstract thing have a physical form. Choose an object that would be ordinary in any other scene, so the weight comes from the moment rather than from the prop.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: Crime, Drama, Gangster, Family Drama, Heritage, Tragedy, Thriller
**Avoid when:** The object is symbolic rather than functional. An object that exists only to mean something announces itself, and the audience reads the writer instead of the scene.
**Example:**
> He puts the shop keys on the table. Neither of them touches them for the rest of the scene. At the door, she picks them up.

**Yields to:** `scene.handover` — What moves is a duty, not an object.  
`scene.transaction_scene`

### The Threshold Scene

**Also called:** the doorway scene, the scene that does not come inside
**What it is:** An entire scene conducted at a boundary — a doorway, a gate, a car window, a counter, a screen — with one character inside and one outside, and no invitation extended.
**Effect on the audience:** The relationship's status, delivered without a word about it. Whether someone is asked in is the fastest available read on where they stand.
**Used for and where it works best:** Returns, requests, and estrangements. It is the correct shape for any scene about whether someone will be readmitted — to a family, a house, a country, a business — because the physical arrangement states the question the dialogue can then avoid. It is also unusually cheap to shoot, which makes it valuable in low-budget and AI-generated work.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Short Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Vertical Micro-Drama, Stage Play | genres: Family Drama, Drama, Social Drama, Heritage, Crime, Migration, Romance
**Avoid when:** The characters have an existing intimacy that makes the boundary artificial. If she would obviously come in, keeping her out is the writer's decision rather than the character's.
**Example:**
> Eleven years. He stands on the step the entire time. She holds the door at the same angle for the entire scene, and when she finally opens it wider, he says he has to go.

**Yields to:** `scene.arrival_scene` — Existing intimacy makes the boundary artificial.  
`scene.threshold_scene`

### The Interrupted Ritual

**Also called:** breaking the ceremony, the disrupted form
**What it is:** A scene set inside a ritual with known steps — a meal, a prayer, a wedding, a funeral, a graduation, a shift handover — which is broken partway through by something that does not belong.
**Effect on the audience:** Shock out of proportion to the event, because a ritual creates an expectation the audience did not know they had until it was violated.
**Used for and where it works best:** Turning points in stories about community, family or faith. The ritual must be shown working correctly first, for long enough to establish its rhythm — usually longer than feels necessary. The break should come from a participant rather than an outsider; a stranger disrupting a ritual is an intrusion, but a member doing it is a rupture.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Stage Play, Heritage Documentary, Short Film | genres: Family Drama, Heritage, Historical, Faith, Tragedy, Social Drama, War
**Avoid when:** The audience does not know the ritual. If the correct form is unfamiliar, the break is invisible — either teach the form in an earlier scene or choose a ritual the audience already holds.
**Example:**
> The whole table waits while the eldest says the blessing. He gets to the third line, stops, and asks who moved his father's chair.

**Yields to:** `scene.interrupted_scene` — Audience does not know the form of the ritual.  
`scene.interrupted_ritual`

### The Scene Played Twice

**Also called:** the repeated scene with one change, the return
**What it is:** A scene from earlier in the work is played again — same location, same participants, often near-identical dialogue — with exactly one element altered.
**Effect on the audience:** The entire distance travelled, delivered in the length of one scene. The audience measures the change themselves, which is far stronger than being told about it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Endings, and the close of any series or season. The rule that makes it work is severity of restraint: change one thing only. Two changes and the audience stops measuring and starts watching a new scene. The strongest single change is which character now occupies which position.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Short Film, Animation Feature | genres: Drama, Tragedy, Coming of Age, Family Drama, Heritage, Romance, Crime
**Avoid when:** The first version was not memorable enough to be recognised. The original must be distinctive — a specific location, a specific line, a specific arrangement of bodies — or the return lands as repetition.
**Example:**
> Scene 3: the father at the head of the table, the son standing to serve.
> Scene 61: the same table, the same food, the same words. The son is sitting at the head. Nobody remarks on it.

**Yields to:** `scene.match_join` — The original scene was not distinctive.  
`scene.played_twice`
